<summary>Tool use: **WebFetch**</summary>
 `https://github.com/Luisnvb/fm1-shed/blob/main/SHED_SPEC.md`

```text
## Question delivery and answering

- **Structure:** Each question starts with a cadence in the current key (ii-V-I with sevenths by default, or I-IV-V-I triads at beginner levels), then the stimulus, then the response, then feedback.
- **Stimuli:** Exercise #1 plays a cadence and one note. #2 plays a reference note and a second note, and #3 plays two notes together. #4 plays a cadence and a chord. #5 plays a 7 chord with one note on top. #6 plays an arpeggio, #7 a scale over a bass pedal, #8 a 2–4 chord progression, and #9 a 3–8 note phrase over a vamp.
- **Keys:** The key rotates by circle of fourths on every question in Phase 2. Fixed and random rotation are also defined as options.
- **Controls:** PLAY repeats the stimulus, SEQ repeats the cadence, EDIT reveals the answer (counted as a miss), ARP skips (unscored), and ENV switches exercise type. GLO confirms a dial choice.
- **Keyboard answers:** Degree, interval, and sequence exercises use the 27 keys (F3..G5). Arpeggio, bass, and dictation take a sequence of key presses.
- **Dial answers:** Chord quality, tension, and scale use the PRESETS dial (`encoders[6]`) to pick from a list, then GLO to confirm.
- **Menu:** The PRESETS dial scrolls the 10-entry list (9 exercises plus VAMP MODE), and PLAY starts the selection.
- **Feedback:** A correct answer shows a check and the answer. A miss shows "IT WAS X" and the correct key lights up. Sequence misses show "REACHED n/m". Exercises 1–9 replay the correct answer after a miss.

## Evaluation

- Answers compare by pitch class (octave-independent) unless the exercise says otherwise. Intervals compare the exact note, since telling a 9th from a 2nd needs the octave.
- Sequence answers advance one correct note at a time and fail on the first wrong note.

## Scoring and adaptive difficulty

- A session is 20 questions. The session tracks asked, correct, current streak, and best streak.
- Difficulty goes up one level after 5 straight hits and down one level after 3 straight misses, clamped to the valid range. The spec phrases these as "additional" hits and misses, which is ambiguous, so confirm the exact counting in code.
- The summary is meant to show percent correct and most-missed items. The spec doesn't detail the final summary layout.

## Spaced repetition

- Each item gets a score keyed by exercise type and pool index, stored in RAM and reset every session. Nothing is persisted.
- Only exercises with a bounded pool use it: degree (#1), chord quality (#4), tension (#5), and scale (#7). The rest are purely random.
- A hit raises the score. A miss lowers it by 2, so missed items come back sooner. The spec doesn't give the hit increment.
- `pick()` chooses the lowest-scoring item 60% of the time, breaking ties randomly. The other 40% is uniform random, so the session still reviews the full pool.

## Display layout

- The screen is 240×240 px, RGB565. The app draws in 16-row bands with `fm1_screen_blit` and its own 5×7 font.
- **Menu:** A header with the title and key, then a scrollable list with a cursor (`>`).
- **Question:** A title with a counter (e.g., "7/20"), the prompt, a stimulus line, a "Play the answer" hint, button hints (`[REP] [CAD] [REV] [>]`), and a footer with streak and level.
- **Vamp:** The vamp name, NOW and NEXT chords, suggested SCALE, and VIEW, plus button hints.
- **Key LEDs:** Buttons use LEDs 0–13 and note keys use 14–40. In vamp views, solid means chord tones and blinking means available tensions, with blink timing based on `now/300`.

## Data tables and format

- Pure C with `const` tables and no `malloc`. Pitch classes run 0–11 with C = 0, and intervals are semitone offsets from the root.
- **Chord types:** Interval lists such as maj7 = `0 4 7 11`.
- **Scales:** Interval lists, such as Dorian = `0 2 3 5 7 9 10`.
- **Chord→scale:** A table keyed by chord and function context. A lookup falls back to the chord's generic row and returns `NULL` if none exists.
- **Vamps:** `struct fm1_shed_vamp_step { chord, context, offset, duration_ms }`, with offsets relative to the active key.
- **Exercise enum:** `fm1_shed_exercise_type`, with exercise pool accessors such as `fm1_shed_X_pool_size/at(level, index)`.
- Host tests check the theory tables against the document and confirm every vamp chord resolves to a real lookup row.

## Note spelling

The spec doesn't define a spelling approach. Internally, everything uses pitch classes. Spelled names appear only in screen labels such as "Ab", "B", or "Bb" in the mockup, and chord and scale names are symbolic (♭9, ♯11). It doesn't say how enharmonic spellings (flats vs. sharps) are chosen per key, so that rule would need to be defined.
```

Links: [{"title":"Learning melodic musical intervals: To block or to interleave?","url":"https://ink.library.smu.edu.sg/soss_research/4316"},{"title":"sage.cnpereading.com","url":"https://sage.cnpereading.com/doi/10.1177/0305735620922595"},{"title":"sciencegate.app","url":"https://www.sciencegate.app/keyword/265981"},{"title":"Journal article","url":"https://findanexpert.unimelb.edu.au/scholarlywork/1493106-learning-music-composers'-styles--to-block-or-to-interleave%3F"},{"title":"Learning Music Composers’ Styles: To Block or to Interleave?","url":"https://bvbvf1.bib-bvb.de/vufind/PrimoRecord/cdi_proquest_journals_2412504899"},{"title":"Learning Music Composers’ Styles: To Block or to Interleave?","url":"https://www.bohrium.com/paper-details/learning-music-composers-styles-to-block-or-to-interleave/812649903640543233-5172"},{"title":"Learning Music Composers’ Styles: To Block or to Interleave?","url":"https://bvbvf1.bib-bvb.de/vufind/PrimoRecord/cdi_proquest_journals_2412504899/Details"},{"title":"Publication Type","url":"https://ink.library.smu.edu.sg/soss_research/4307"},{"title":"DOI: 10.1177/87551233261474481 ISSN: 8755-1233","url":"https://www.citedrive.com/en/discovery/comparing-interleaved-and-blocked-practices-in-secondary-school-music-performances/"},{"title":"Music teacher","url":"https://colindorman.com/?p=3977"}]

The paper is Wong, Chen & Lim (2021), published in *Psychology of Music* 49(4), pp. 1027–1046, DOI 10.1177/0305735620922595. The abstract is available through the SMU institutional repository and a SAGE mirror.

**Main findings:**
- **Experiment 1:** When participants had familiar reference songs and singing as support, blocked and interleaved practice gave about the same results on a test of novel examples of the trained intervals. interleaving and blocking yielded comparable performance on a test requiring participants to classify novel instances of the studied interval types.
- **Experiment 2:** Without those aids, interleaving clearly won. The abstract reports that interleaving produced superior musical interval identification than blocking.
- **Metacognition:** Most learners did not recognize the advantage. most participants were unaware of the benefits of interleaving, and misjudged blocking to be more effective.

**Design:** Novices learned six interval types in an interleaved schedule and six in a blocked schedule within a single session, using a programmed intervention. The abstract also notes the authors' finding that the benefit depends on context, which the ScienceGate listing describes as the potential influence of context under which interleaving is a beneficial technique for learning melodic musical intervals.

**Related work:** The same group's 2020 *Journal of Research in Music Education* study on composer styles found a similar interleaving advantage, with most participants again misjudging blocking as more effective (Wong, Low, Kang & Lim, 2020).

I only ran one search, so I did not check the full text or other citing papers.

**Authors:** Francisco Veniel-Martí, Ana María Botella-Nicolás, Diana Omigie, and María Herrojo-Ruiz

**Journal:** Not named on the page. It lists only the ISSN (8755-1233) and DOI (10.1177/87551233261474481).

**Year:** Not stated. The "Release Year" field is blank.

**Design:**
- Intact groups of first-year secondary students (N = 60)
- An 11-session, 5-week, teacher-led intervention comparing interleaved and blocked practice schedules
- Students practiced four similar melodic pieces on the recorder
- Performance was assessed at pretest, posttest, and a 4-week follow-up using a performance rubric

**Main findings:**
- Both groups improved from pretest to posttest, with no significant between-group differences.
- At follow-up, the interleaving group maintained its performance levels, while the blocked group showed a significant decline.
- The authors conclude that "teacher-directed interleaving may support longer-term retention of music performance skills" in secondary general music classrooms.

<tool-use data-tool-type="shell" data-tool-name="Bash"><details>
<summary>Tool use: **Bash**</summary>
Read docs rules and firmware rules in AGENTS.md

`sed -n 100,130p AGENTS.md; sed -n 240,260p AGENTS.md`

```text
Prefer these recipes over calling M-Flasher directly. There is deliberately no
recipe for `bootloader`, `restore` or `run-ram`.

Run `just docs-check` before committing any change under `docs/` or to
`zensical.toml`. Pushing to `main` deploys the site.

## Writing conventions

- `docs/**` is written in **Traditional Chinese (Taiwan usage)**. Keep technical
  terms, identifiers, CLI commands, button names (`REC`, `OCT-`), product and
  repo names in English. Use 程式/檔案/設定/資料, not Mainland variants.
- `AGENTS.md`, `README.md`, commit messages, code comments: English.
- The site is single-language. Do not add locale-suffixed pages.
- Every new page must be added to `nav` in `zensical.toml`.
- Version numbers live in `docs/resources.md`. Other pages link there instead of
  repeating them, except where a procedure pins a specific version.
- Dated facts use absolute dates (`2026-11-17`), never "recently".

## Capture what we learn

When a question in the session produces an answer worth keeping — how to do
something on the device, why something behaves a certain way, a pitfall, a
working setup — add it to the relevant page under `docs/` in the same turn,
without being asked. Put it where a reader would look for it (the firmware's
own chapter, `hardware/`, `getting-started/`), tag it (`[實機]`, `[上游]`,
`[模擬]`, `[調研]`), and mention in the reply which page changed. Do not record
one-off chatter or things already written down.

## Sources and evidence


The daemon presses keys in real agent sessions. When testing, send keys only to
terminals the test started itself (`just cond-it` labels them `conductor-test=1`
and kills them after). Never approve, deny or interrupt the owner's own agents
from a test. There is no auto-approve; do not add one without the owner asking.

## Not set up yet

A repo-owned skill for operating the unit and an `fm1` CLI wrapper (the `Justfile` covers it for now;
`fm1-hub-listing` covers publishing only). `fm1-emu` is a downloaded binary, not a source checkout.
A vocabulary app is at the idea stage (`docs/dev/vocab.md`). A deck written to the flash data area would need
the firmware-development rule "never compute flash addresses or call erase/program directly" changed first,
with the owner's approval; the proposed wording is in that page.
```
</details></tool-use>

static inline uint16_t swap16(uint32_t c) { return (uint16_t)(((c >> 8) & 0xFFu) | ((c & 0xFFu) << 8)); }

static void cv_begin(uint32_t w, uint32_t h, uint16_t bg)
{
    uint32_t i, n;
    if (w * h > CV_MAX)
        h = CV_MAX / w;
    lcd_sync();                     /* the last blit may still read cv_px */
    cv_w = w;
    cv_h = h;
    cv_oy = cv_y0 = 0;
    cv_y1 = (int32_t)h;
    n = w * h;
    for (i = 0; i < n; i++)
        cv_px[i] = swap16(bg);
}

/* X0X: draw the next things as if the canvas were rows y0 .. y0+h-1 alone (one band of a
 * canvas that holds several, sent in one transfer so the bands change on screen together) */
static void cv_band(int32_t y0, int32_t h)
static int32_t text_w(const felucca_font_t *f, const char *s)
{
    int32_t w = 0;
    for (; *s; s++)
        w += f->adv[glyph(f, (uint8_t)*s)];
    return w;
}

/* one-shot: text in a box, cleared to black, blitted */
static void draw_text_box(uint32_t x, uint32_t y, uint32_t w, const felucca_font_t *f, const char *s,
                          uint16_t c, int align)
{
    int32_t tw = text_w(f, s), tx = 0;
    cv_begin(w, f->h, C_BLACK);
    if (align == 1)
        tx = ((int32_t)w - tw) / 2;
    else if (align == 2)
        tx = (int32_t)w - tw;
    cv_text(tx, 0, f, s, c);
    cv_blit(x, y);
    lcd_sync();                     /* one-shots (boot, crash, UBOOT, update) finish here */
}

"""Pack the SRAM load images for boot and verify their decoder's XIP closure."""
import lzma
import re
import struct

MAGIC = 0x31414D4C  # LMA1: device/boot_lzma.h BOOT_LZMA_MAGIC
# Raw LZMA1, as boot_lzma.h decodes it: lc 1, lp 1, pb 1 (instructions are
# halfword aligned), with the end marker. The dictionary is the whole image.
FILTERS = [{'id': lzma.FILTER_LZMA1, 'preset': 9 | lzma.PRESET_EXTREME,
            'lc': 1, 'lp': 1, 'pb': 1, 'dict_size': 1 << 20}]
# The sections fm1_cstart unpacks, in their load order from _rt_load (device/app.ld, device/main_fm1.c)
SECTIONS = ('ramtext.bin', 'data.bin')


def pack(raw):
    """one load image: [MAGIC, packed bytes, raw bytes, 0], the stream, padded to a word"""
    data = lzma.compress(raw, format=lzma.FORMAT_RAW, filters=FILTERS)
    if lzma.decompress(data, format=lzma.FORMAT_RAW, filters=FILTERS) != raw:
        raise ValueError('boot image compression round trip failed')
    return struct.pack('<4I', MAGIC, len(data), len(raw), 0) + data + b'\0' * (-len(data) % 4)


def pack_images(blobs):
    """every section's load image, one after another (an empty section still has its record)"""

The search didn't turn up a C library for chord and scale spelling. The results cover general spelling theory, plus one unrelated Rust crate.

- **Scale spelling rule:** A properly spelled scale uses each letter name once, so A minor is spelled with the letters A through G. A properly spelt-out scale should feature each letter name only once, eg A, B, C, D, E, F, G for A minor.
- **Enharmonics:** Notes that share a pitch but have different letter names are enharmonic. If two notes have the same pitch but have different letter names, we call them enharmonic.
- **Line of fifths:** The circle of fifths contains all twelve chromatic pitches, with each one a fifth from its neighbor. It's named as such because with the arrangement of the pitches, each note is a 5th apart from the adjacent note. Chord and scale spelling can be derived from positions along that line.
- **Enharmonic scale equivalents:** One source notes that Db major is enharmonically the same as C# major, so the two share pitches but are spelled differently. Enharmonically, the Db major scale is equivalent to the C# major scale: C# D# E# F# G# A# B#.
- **Code example:** The closest match is the Rust crate `harmonia`, which has a spelling module for diatonic scales. Enharmonic spelling for diatonic scales. It requires that each spelled note match the pitch class of its scale tone. Its source is in Rust, not C, and it covers scales only, not chords.

I'd suggest a more specific search, such as "C library music theory note spelling" or "C pitch class spelling library," to find a C implementation.

**Gingoduino** is a music theory engine for embedded systems, described as "Music theory engine for embedded systems." It is a contributed Arduino library by Saulo Verissimo.

===
# Writing music programmatically

Alda is designed to be easy to learn and use, even for those who have little to
no programming experience. The language is deliberately simple, omitting the
complex features that you see in most programming languages, like functions,
classes, and types.

For example, a C major scale played on an acoustic guitar in eighth notes,
starting on C3 _(that's the note C in octave number 3)_ is written like this:

```alda
acoustic-guitar:
  o3 c8 d e f g a b > c
```

At the same time, an important goal of Alda is to facilitate writing music
programmatically. You can get a lot of mileage out of the Alda language alone,
but if you happen to have a little bit of programming knowledge, you can go
beyond thinking of Alda as a **language** and start to think of it as a
**platform** for algorithmic composition and live coding.

## What is algorithmic composition?

Simply put, [algorithmic
composition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithmic_composition) is when you
write music in a way that leaves some part of the process up to chance. Which
parts are left up to chance, and how exactly the "chance" parts are implemented,
is entirely open-ended.

For example, you could write a piece of music where you come up with a set of
rhythms, as well as a set of pitches, and then you write a computer program that
puts together random combinations of the rhythms and pitches to create a piece
of music.

Another example: you could write a program that fetches the 10-day weather
forecast for your area and uses some arbitrary rules to convert it into music.
For instance, maybe if the temperature is an odd number, a major scale will be
used; or maybe if the forecast calls for snow, one of the instruments will be a
cello; etc.

===
# Implementing an Alda library

The article on [writing music programmatically][writing-music-programmatically]
explains how Alda is designed to be controlled easily by other programming
languages. The idea is that Alda is intended to be not just a simple
**language** for music composition, but also a **platform** for the programmatic
creation of music.

This simplicity in the design of Alda gives programmers the freedom to create
libraries for driving Alda in just about any programming language that they want
to use.

If you're interested in helping to extend support for Alda to users of your
programming language of choice, read on!

## Example: alda-clj

The Clojure library [alda-clj] is the canonical reference implementation of a
programming language library for Alda. Dave Yarwood (who is also the creator of
Alda) wrote alda-clj with the goal of being able to write Clojure code that will
generate interesting musical scores by taking random or "found" data (e.g.
weather forecasts) and translating it into Alda source code.

Here are a couple of basic examples showing how you can use alda-clj in a
Clojure program or REPL session:

```clojure
;; Import all of the functions from alda.core into the current context
(require '[alda.core :refer :all])
````

The results don't use the term "Scale chord." On the MK4, the chord options are Chord Map, User Chord, and Fixed Chord, and Scale mode is a separate feature that these chord modes work with.

- **Scale mode:** The MK4 offers 30 scales. One user guide describes three Scale sub-modes: Snap to Scale, which moves out-of-key notes to the nearest in-key note, and Easy Scale, which maps the scale onto the white keys. A third, Filter Out of Scale, appears in another Novation article. The Scale mode is used to keep playing in key. Scale mode allows you to pick a scale and your Launchkey helps you play in that scale more easily. In Snap to Scale mode, your Launchkey rounds any note outside the Scale to the nearest note in the chosen scale. In Easy Scale mode, your Launchkey maps all the notes in your chosen scale to your Launchkey's white keys.
- **Chord Map:** With a scale selected, Chord Map turns the pads into a set of chords that fit the scale. In Chord Map mode, your Launchkey's pads and encoders enable you to perform chords that fit with the Scale you select.
- **User Chord:** You assign your own chords to the pads. User Chord mode allows you to input your own chords. To assign one, press an empty pad and play the notes you want on the keyboard.
- **Fixed Chord:** You record a chord once and play it from a single key, transposed across the keyboard. 'Fixed Chord' is similar, but this time, you are assigning a chord to the keyboard that can be played and transposed on every key. Novation's own material adds that activating Scale Mode lets you transpose your chord while staying perfectly in key.

Sources for the 49-key model are thin. Novation's user guide for the MK4 49 has dedicated Scale and Chord Mode sections, but the search only returned its table of contents, so I could not confirm the exact button steps for that model.

Both products use lit keys to guide practice, but they differ in how they handle waiting and pacing.

**Casio:** The LK-S250 has a Key Lighting System that guides you by lighting the next key to play, and the Step Up Lesson function, which helps you practice in a four-step format. In the Casio lesson system, the keyboard can wait for you to find the right notes before continuing. An older Casio manual describes the same behavior for its 3-Step Lesson modes, where accompaniment waits for correct input from you before proceeding. For the LK-S450, a listing says its Step-Up Lesson Mode with 160 songs and exercises lets you control how quickly you move through the levels.

**ROLI LUMI Keys:** The LUMI app has a catalog of songs, and each of the keys light up when you're meant to be hitting them. A review says you can also use the Wait mode in Practice which silences the backing and lets you play in your own time. The ROLI Dashboard handles setup, and your LUMI can store four different Modes at once which can be toggled by pressing the Power button.

**Key difference:** Casio's lesson mode is built around the keyboard waiting for correct input at each step. ROLI's Wait mode is a practice option that removes the backing track so you can play at your own pace. The sources don't directly compare how the two handle a missed note.

<summary>Tool use: **WebFetch**</summary>
 `https://www.fourmilab.ch/webtools/midicsv/`

````text
**License:** midicsv is in the public domain. The document states, "This software is in the public domain." It also grants permission to use, copy, modify, and distribute the software and its documentation for any purpose without fee, and says it is provided "as is" without warranty.

**CSV record format:** Each record has at least three leading fields: Track number, Time (in MIDI clocks), and Type. Type-specific parameters follow. For a Note_on_c event, the parameters are Channel, Note, and Velocity. Note 60 is middle C, and velocity ranges from 0 to 127. A Note_off_c record uses the same parameters, with velocity normally set to 0.

Example lines:

```
2, 960, Note_on_c, 1, 81, 81
2, 1920, Note_off_c, 1, 81, 0
```

These lines mean that on track 2, at time 960, channel 1 plays note 81 with velocity 81, and at time 1920 it stops that note.
````

I've finished the research. A few items could not be confirmed and are marked **[unverified]**. Licence statements were checked on the source pages unless noted.

# Best-practice report: keyboard and theory trainer for the FM-1

## 1. Learning-science principles applied to music

**Interleaving (mixing items) vs blocking (one item at a time)**
- **Carter & Grahn 2016** (*Frontiers in Psychology* 7:1251). 10 advanced clarinettists practised one pair of pieces in 12-minute blocks and another pair in 3-minute alternating segments. Where judges heard a difference, the interleaved pieces were rated better. The players found interleaving more useful for focus and for spotting errors, but most still preferred blocking. https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2016.01251/full
- **Wong, Chen & Lim 2021** (*Psychology of Music* 49(4):1027–1046). Novices learned melodic intervals. When they had reference songs and singing to help, interleaving and blocking scored about the same. Without those aids, interleaving was clearly better. Most learners wrongly believed blocking worked better. https://ink.library.smu.edu.sg/soss_research/4316
- **Pavlik et al. 2013** (EDM conference). Learners telling tritones from octaves did better when the practice trials were interleaved. The paper also models spacing and forgetting. https://digitalcommons.memphis.edu/facpubs/8219
- **Veniel-Martí et al.** (*Update: Applications of Research in Music Education*, probably 2026 based on the DOI **[year unverified]**). 60 secondary-school recorder students. There was no difference at the posttest. At a 4-week follow-up the interleaved group held its level and the blocked group declined. https://www.citedrive.com/en/discovery/comparing-interleaved-and-blocked-practices-in-secondary-school-music-performances/
- Practical rule: block briefly when an item is new, then interleave. The benefit is reported to depend on how similar the items are (Brunmair & Richter 2019 meta-analysis **[not read directly]**).

**Spaced repetition (FSRS/Anki)**
- I found no peer-reviewed study of Anki or FSRS for music theory. Community decks exist:
  - Free ear-training decks: https://girlinbluemusic.com/product/free-ear-training-anki-decks/
  - A jazz-practice Anki write-up: https://malcolmsailor.github.io/2023/11/22/anki-for-jazz-practice.html
- Long-term users report that spaced repetition suits facts (key signatures, chord spellings) better than motor skills: https://medium.com/@tomargames/anki-for-music-after-5-years-d518a640676c
- FSRS has been built into Anki since version 23.10. Implementations:
  - MIT licence: py-fsrs, ts-fsrs, rs-fsrs
  - BSD-3-Clause: fsrs-rs, according to its metadata
  - https://github.com/open-spaced-repetition — check each repo's LICENSE file before using it.
- My own inference: the FSRS scheduler alone (without the optimiser) needs only a few numbers per card, so it should fit on a microcontroller.

**Deliberate practice**
- It matters, but less than claimed. It explains about 21% of the variance in music performance (Macnamara et al. 2014): https://www.psychologie.uzh.ch/dam/jcr:658d39fe-2f4b-467f-9ae2-ffeb25caf2b6/McNamara.PsychSci.25.2014.pdf
- A music-only meta-analysis put it at about 37% after correcting for measurement error (Platz et al. 2014): https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.00646/pdf

**How you practise matters more than how long**
- **Duke, Simmons & Cash 2009** (*JRME* 56(4)). 17 advanced pianists. Total practice time and number of repetitions did not predict next-day retention. The best players found the exact error spots, fixed them, and varied tempo on purpose. https://cml.music.utexas.edu/research/skill-learning-and-procedural-memory
- Sleep and 24-hour gaps between sessions help keyboard-sequence learning (Simmons & Duke 2006, *JRME* 54:257–269) **[secondary summaries only]**.

**Short sessions**
- The UT Austin Center for Music Learning advises:
  - split an hour into 2–3 sessions
  - stop before you want to
  - rotate goals about every 5 minutes
  - change one thing at a time
- This is a lab's practical guidance, not trial evidence. https://cml.music.utexas.edu/online-resources/intelligent-music-practice/10-tips-for-effective-practice
- Motor-learning reviews recommend shorter, more frequent sessions, but the best session length is not established.

**Slow practice and tempo ladders**
- Allingham & Wöllner 2022 (*Psychology of Music*): nearly all musicians use slow practice and find it useful, but there is little experimental evidence for it. Slow and fast movements may also be organised differently, so a tempo ladder should reach, and sometimes pass, the target tempo. https://ediss.sub.uni-hamburg.de/handle/ediss/9763
- I found no study testing "tempo ladders" as such.
- **Chunking:** widely taught, but I found no music-specific controlled study **[unverified]**.

## 2. Ear training pedagogy

**Reference songs.** These mostly cover ascending melodic intervals and are tied to particular scale degrees: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interval_recognition. Wong 2021 suggests interleaving matters most once those song crutches are removed.

**Functional ear training**
- Alain Benbassat's Functional Ear Trainer plays a cadence (I–IV–V–I), then a note, and you name its scale degree. The apps are free:
  - https://apps.apple.com/app/id1088761926
  - https://sourceforge.net/app/functional-ear-trainer/
- Bruce Arnold's *Ear Training One Note* (Muse Eek) also plays a cadence then one pitch. He suggests moving to his next volume at about 50% accuracy. https://brucearnold.com/?p=794
- **Miles Okazaki:** I did not search for or verify an ear-training method by him **[unverified]**.

**Academic aural-skills courses**
- Chenette, *Foundations of Aural Skills* (2022, CC BY-SA). Order: Attention → Meter → Tonic/Collection & Solfège (find the tonic, movable-do) → Materiality → Memory. https://uen.pressbooks.pub/auralskills/
- Berklee Ear Training 1 covers movable-do, melodies, intervals and harmony in major keys. Ear Training 2 moves to minor keys. https://college.berklee.edu/node/2270561
- Lake ("Interval and Scale-Degree Strategies in Melodic Perception", *JMTP*) finds scale-degree hearing best for tonal melodies, with intervals still needed and listeners switching between the two **[full text not read]**.
- I found no controlled study directly comparing functional and interval training. The consensus comes from teachers and textbooks.

**Common order:**
1. Find the tonic, then hear degrees 1-3-5, then all diatonic degrees, each after a cadence
2. Intervals heard inside a key: ascending, then descending, then harmonic
3. Triad quality: major/minor, then diminished/augmented
4. Bass degree and recognising I/IV/V/vi progressions
5. Seventh chords
6. Minor keys and chromatic degrees
7. Short melodic dictation (3–5 notes)

Train relative pitch, not absolute pitch.

## 3. Keyboard skills curricula

**ABRSM 2025–26 piano scales** (unchanged since the 2021 overhaul). Mirror of the specification: https://caswells-strings.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/ABRSM-Piano-syllabus-2025-2026.pdf

| Level | Keys and requirement |
|---|---|
| Initial | C major, D minor, 1 octave, hands separately |
| Grade 1 | G, F major; A, D minor, 2 octaves, hands separately |
| Grade 2 | Grade 1 keys hands together; new: D, A major; E, G minor, hands separately |
| Grade 3 | Grade 2's new keys hands together; new: B♭, E♭ major; B, C minor, hands separately |
| Grade 4 | Grade 3's new keys hands together; new: B, F♯, A♭ major; F♯, F minor, hands separately |
| Grade 5 | A, E, B, F♯, D♭ major; F♯, C♯, G♯, E♭, B♭ minor, hands together |
| Grades 6–8 | All keys again, plus scales a 3rd or 6th apart |

- Speed marks rise from ♩=54 (Initial) to ♩=100 (Grade 4).
- The pattern is a spiral: new keys hands separately, then hands together the next grade. Keys spread outward from C on both sides of the circle of fifths rather than going strictly around it.
- RCM 2022 Level 1 uses C, G, F major and A, E, D minor (third-party chart): https://colorinmypiano.com/wp-content/files/RCM_2022_Technical_Requirements_Charts_Prep-10.pdf

**FM-1 implication:** 25 keys is exactly two octaves (C to C). Two-octave scales hands together won't fit, so use one octave or the octave-shift buttons.

**Keyboard harmony and pop piano**
- Left hand plays the root, an octave, or an open fifth. Right hand plays triad inversions, moving each note to the nearest note of the next chord (voice leading).
  - https://hub.yamaha.com/poprock-voicings-part-1
  - https://pianowithjonny.com/piano-lessons/pop-piano-accompaniment-popstinatos/
- Then add left-hand patterns such as root-fifth-octave and broken chords: https://www.dummies.com/article/academics-the-arts/music/instruments/piano/great-left-hand-accompaniment-patterns-for-the-piano-or-keyboard-153052/
- For ii–V–I, use jazz shell voicings (root-3-7 or root-7): https://www.pianogroove.com/?p=11596
- **Fingering systems:** I did not research these specifically **[not sourced here]**.

**Nashville Number System**
- Chords written as scale-degree numbers, usually in 4-bar lines; a minor key's 1 chord is noted as minor. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville_Number_System
- De Clercq 2019 (*JMTP*) compares it with Roman numerals: https://www.midside.com/publications/declercq_2019_jmtp.pdf

## 4. Pop/contemporary theory for arranging

**Hooktheory statistics**
- I–V–vi–IV is the most common four-chord progression (1,300-song analysis, 2012): https://www.hooktheory.com/blog/i-analyzed-the-chords-of-1300-popular-songs-for-patterns-this-is-what-i-found/
- The Trends API example data shows the share of all chords: I 17.6%, IV 12%, V 11.6%, vi 7.5%, ii 3.3%. After IV, the next chord is I 33% of the time and V 27%. https://hooktheory.com/api/trends/docs
- Inversions change what follows: after G/B, the move to vi jumps from 29% to 61%. https://www.hooktheory.com/blog/statistical-study-inversions-slash-chords-popular-music/

**Open Music Theory pop chapters** (CC BY-SA)
- Covers: Blues-Based, Four-Chord, Classical (Lament), Puff and Modal schemas; Pentatonic Harmony; Fragile/Absent Tonics.
- Doo-wop is I–vi–IV–V; singer/songwriter is vi–IV–I–V.
- https://viva.pressbooks.pub/openmusictheory/chapter/4-chord-schemas/

**Royal Road (王道進行)**
- IVM7–V7–iii7–vi, often extended with ii7–V7–I. Minor form: VIM7–VII7–v7–i.
- As of 2023, 40% of Japan's top-20 best-selling singles use it.
- The related Komuro progression is vi–IV–V–I.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_road_progression
- Use in Mandopop and Cantopop: the Wikipedia table lists many Chinese songs, mostly uncited. A Bilibili article links 4536251 to Jay Chou ballads from 七里香 onward: https://www.bilibili.com/read/cv2277428/ **[secondary sources]**.

**Other topics**
- Andalusian cadence i–♭VII–♭VI–V: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andalusian_cadence
- Modal mixture (borrowing from the parallel minor, e.g. iv, ♭VI, ♭VII in major): https://viva.pressbooks.pub/openmusictheory/chapter/modal-mixture/
- OMT also covers secondary (applied) dominants and blues schemas.

**Hooktheory licence: not usable.**
- The Terms of Service page I fetched says "Last updated October, 2026". It forbids copying, scraping, bulk download, text-and-data mining or redistribution of the TheoryTab database unless Hooktheory gives a written data licence. https://www.hooktheory.com/terms
- The API needs an account, is limited to 10 requests per 10 seconds, publishes no licence, and offers no data dump.
- Citing published aggregate findings (like "I–V–vi–IV is most common") should be fine, since facts aren't copyrightable. This is a general principle, not legal advice.

## 5. Free / openly licensed sources

| Source | Licence | Usable in GPL/MIT firmware? |
|---|---|---|
| Open Music Theory v2 | CC BY-SA 4.0, "except where otherwise noted" | GPLv3 only, one-way (https://creativecommons.org/2015/10/08/cc-by-sa-4-0-now-one-way-compatible-with-gplv3/). Not MIT or GPLv2 except as separately licensed files |
| musictheory.net | Lesson **text and still images: CC BY 4.0**. Lesson data/JSON, player, source code, audio/samples and apps are proprietary (https://musictheory.net/legal) | Text and images: yes, with attribution. FSF says CC BY 4.0 is compatible with all GPL versions (https://www.gnu.org/licenses/license-list.html) |
| teoria.com | CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (footer) | No. FSF classes NC and ND as nonfree |
| Wikipedia | CC BY-SA 4.0 since June 2023 (https://creativecommons.org/2023/06/29/wikipedia-moves-to-cc-4-0-licenses/) | GPLv3 only |
| Hutchinson, *Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom* | GFDL | GFDL is not GPL-compatible **[FSF FAQ, not re-checked]** |
| Chenette, *Foundations of Aural Skills* | CC BY-SA (version not verified) | Like OMT |
| Schmidt-Jones, *Understanding Basic Music Theory* | CC BY (version reported as 2.0 or 3.0) | Yes, with attribution |
| Mount, *Fundamentals, Function, and Form* | CC BY-NC 4.0 | No |
| Baylor *Ear Training Compendium* | CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 | No |
| Hooktheory TheoryTab | Proprietary | No |
| Berklee courses | No open licence found | Treat as proprietary |

The cleanest option: scale formulas, fingerings and progressions are facts, so write original content and use OMT and musictheory.net as references. In an MIT-licensed repo, keep any CC content in separate files under its own licence.

## 6. Suggested topic progression (adult beginner to intermediate)

This blends ABRSM's spiral, Berklee's major-then-minor order, Chenette's tonic-first approach and Hooktheory's chord frequencies. Each stage mixes theory, keyboard, ear and a pop application. Use interleaved review and spaced repetition throughout.

1. **Foundations.** Keyboard layout, whole and half steps, major-scale formula. C, G, F major one octave, hands separately then together. Ear: hear the tonic, then degrees 1-3-5 after a cadence.
2. **Diatonic triads.** Chords I to vii° in C, G and F, written in Roman and Nashville numbers. Play I–IV–V–I with nearest-voice inversions: left hand root, right hand triad. Ear: major vs minor triads. Pop: I–V–vi–IV, vi–IV–I–V, I–vi–IV–V.
3. **Circle of fifths and key signatures** (flashcards with spaced repetition). Add D, A, B♭, E♭ major and the relative minors A, E, D (natural and harmonic). Ear: all diatonic degrees, and intervals heard inside a key. Recognise I/IV/V/vi progressions.
4. **Sevenths and minor keys.** V7, ii–V–I, the four seventh-chord qualities, shell voicings, 12-bar blues, Andalusian cadence, Royal Road. Ear: chord quality, and bass degree.
5. **All 12 keys.** Remaining scales and arpeggios. Play I–IV–V–I and ii–V–I in every key, transposing around the circle. Ear: descending and harmonic intervals, inversions, 3–5 note melodic dictation.
6. **Colour.** Secondary dominants (V/V, V/vi), modal mixture (iv, ♭VI, ♭VII), pentatonic and blues scales, Mixolydian/Dorian/Lydian as pop flavours. Slash-chord bass lines and left-hand patterns. Ear: chromatic degrees and borrowed chords.
7. **Ongoing.** 10–20 minute interleaved sessions, tempo ladders that reach and pass the target, and spaced-repetition review of facts.

- Alain Benbassat's Functional Ear Trainer plays a cadence (I–IV–V–I), then a note, and you name its scale degree. The apps are free:
  - https://apps.apple.com/app/id1088761926
  - https://sourceforge.net/app/functional-ear-trainer/
- Bruce Arnold's *Ear Training One Note* (Muse Eek) also plays a cadence then one pitch. He suggests moving to his next volume at about 50% accuracy. https://brucearnold.com/?p=794
- **Miles Okazaki:** I did not search for or verify an ear-training method by him **[unverified]**.

**Academic aural-skills courses**
- Chenette, *Foundations of Aural Skills* (2022, CC BY-SA). Order: Attention → Meter → Tonic/Collection &amp; Solfège (find the tonic, movable-do) → Materiality → Memory. https://uen.pressbooks.pub/auralskills/
- Berklee Ear Training 1 covers movable-do, melodies, intervals and harmony in major keys. Ear Training 2 moves to minor keys. https://college.berklee.edu/node/2270561
- Lake ("Interval and Scale-Degree Strategies in Melodic Perception", *JMTP*) finds scale-degree hearing best for tonal melodies, with intervals still needed and listeners switching between the two **[full text not read]**.
- I found no controlled study directly comparing functional and interval training. The consensus comes from teachers and textbooks.

**Common order:**
1. Find the tonic, then hear degrees 1-3-5, then all diatonic degrees, each after a cadence
2. Intervals heard inside a key: ascending, then descending, then harmonic
3. Triad quality: major/minor, then diminished/augmented
4. Bass degree and recognising I/IV/V/vi progressions
5. Seventh chords
6. Minor keys and chromatic degrees
7. Short melodic dictation (3–5 notes)

Train relative pitch, not absolute pitch.

## 3. Keyboard skills curricula

**ABRSM 2025–26 piano scales** (unchanged since the 2021 overhaul). Mirror of the specification: https://caswells-strings.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/ABRSM-Piano-syllabus-2025-2026.pdf

| Level | Keys and requirement |
|---|---|
| Initial | C major, D minor, 1 octave, hands separately |
| Grade 1 | G, F major; A, D minor, 2 octaves, hands separately |
| Grade 2 | Grade 1 keys hands together; new: D, A major; E, G minor, hands separately |
| Grade 3 | Grade 2's new keys hands together; new: B♭, E♭ major; B, C minor, hands separately |
| Grade 4 | Grade 3's new keys hands together; new: B, F♯, A♭ major; F♯, F minor, hands separately |
| Grade 5 | A, E, B, F♯, D♭ major; F♯, C♯, G♯, E♭, B♭ minor, hands together |
| Grades 6–8 | All keys again, plus scales a 3rd or 6th apart |

- Speed marks rise from ♩=54 (Initial) to ♩=100 (Grade 4).
- The pattern is a spiral: new keys hands separately, then hands together the next grade. Keys spread outward from C on both sides of the circle of fifths rather than going strictly around it.
- RCM 2022 Level 1 uses C, G, F major and A, E, D minor (third-party chart): https://colorinmypiano.com/wp-content/files/RCM_2022_Technical_Requirements_Charts_Prep-10.pdf

**FM-1 implication:** 25 keys is exactly two octaves (C to C). Two-octave scales hands together won't fit, so use one octave or the octave-shift buttons.

**Keyboard harmony and pop piano**
- Left hand plays the root, an octave, or an open fifth. Right hand plays triad inversions, moving each note to the nearest note of the next chord (voice leading).
  - https://hub.yamaha.com/poprock-voicings-part-1
  - https://pianowithjonny.com/piano-lessons/pop-piano-accompaniment-popstinatos/
- Then add left-hand patterns such as root-fifth-octave and broken chords: https://www.dummies.com/article/academics-the-arts/music/instruments/piano/great-left-hand-accompaniment-patterns-for-the-piano-or-keyboard-153052/
- For ii–V–I, use jazz shell voicings (root-3-7 or root-7): https://www.pianogroove.com/?p=11596
- **Fingering systems:** I did not research these specifically **[not sourced here]**.

**Nashville Number System**
- Chords written as scale-degree numbers, usually in 4-bar lines; a minor key's 1 chord is noted as minor. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville_Number_System
- De Clercq 2019 (*JMTP*) compares it with Roman numerals: https://www.midside.com/publications/declercq_2019_jmtp.pdf

## 4. Pop/contemporary theory for arranging

**Hooktheory statistics**
- I–V–vi–IV is the most common four-chord progression (1,300-song analysis, 2012): https://www.hooktheory.com/blog/i-analyzed-the-chords-of-1300-popular-songs-for-patterns-this-is-what-i-found/
- The Trends API example data shows the share of all chords: I 17.6%, IV 12%, V 11.6%, vi 7.5%, ii 3.3%. After IV, the next chord is I 33% of the time and V 27%. https://hooktheory.com/api/trends/docs
- Inversions change what follows: after G/B, the move to vi jumps from 29% to 61%. https://www.hooktheory.com/blog/statistical-study-inversions-slash-chords-popular-music/

**Open Music Theory pop chapters** (CC BY-SA)
- Covers: Blues-Based, Four-Chord, Classical (Lament), Puff and Modal schemas; Pentatonic Harmony; Fragile/Absent Tonics.
- Doo-wop is I–vi–IV–V; singer/songwriter is vi–IV–I–V.
- https://viva.pressbooks.pub/openmusictheory/chapter/4-chord-schemas/

**Royal Road (王道進行)**
- IVM7–V7–iii7–vi, often extended with ii7–V7–I. Minor form: VIM7–VII7–v7–i.
- As of 2023, 40% of Japan's top-20 best-selling singles use it.
- The related Komuro progression is vi–IV–V–I.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_road_progression
- Use in Mandopop and Cantopop: the Wikipedia table lists many Chinese songs, mostly uncited. A Bilibili article links 4536251 to Jay Chou ballads from 七里香 onward: https://www.bilibili.com/read/cv2277428/ **[secondary sources]**.

**Other topics**
- Andalusian cadence i–♭VII–♭VI–V: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andalusian_cadence
- Modal mixture (borrowing from the parallel minor, e.g. iv, ♭VI, ♭VII in major): https://viva.pressbooks.pub/openmusictheory/chapter/modal-mixture/
- OMT also covers secondary (applied) dominants and blues schemas.

**Hooktheory licence: not usable.**
- The Terms of Service page I fetched says "Last updated October, 2026". It forbids copying, scraping, bulk download, text-and-data mining or redistribution of the TheoryTab database unless Hooktheory gives a written data licence. https://www.hooktheory.com/terms
- The API needs an account, is limited to 10 requests per 10 seconds, publishes no licence, and offers no data dump.
- Citing published aggregate findings (like "I–V–vi–IV is most common") should be fine, since facts aren't copyrightable. This is a general principle, not legal advice.

The cleanest option: scale formulas, fingerings and progressions are facts, so write original content and use OMT and musictheory.net as references. In an MIT-licensed repo, keep any CC content in separate files under its own licence.

## 6. Suggested topic progression (adult beginner to intermediate)

This blends ABRSM's spiral, Berklee's major-then-minor order, Chenette's tonic-first approach and Hooktheory's chord frequencies. Each stage mixes theory, keyboard, ear and a pop application. Use interleaved review and spaced repetition throughout.

1. **Foundations.** Keyboard layout, whole and half steps, major-scale formula. C, G, F major one octave, hands separately then together. Ear: hear the tonic, then degrees 1-3-5 after a cadence.
2. **Diatonic triads.** Chords I to vii° in C, G and F, written in Roman and Nashville numbers. Play I–IV–V–I with nearest-voice inversions: left hand root, right hand triad. Ear: major vs minor triads. Pop: I–V–vi–IV, vi–IV–I–V, I–vi–IV–V.
3. **Circle of fifths and key signatures** (flashcards with spaced repetition). Add D, A, B♭, E♭ major and the relative minors A, E, D (natural and harmonic). Ear: all diatonic degrees, and intervals heard inside a key. Recognise I/IV/V/vi progressions.
4. **Sevenths and minor keys.** V7, ii–V–I, the four seventh-chord qualities, shell voicings, 12-bar blues, Andalusian cadence, Royal Road. Ear: chord quality, and bass degree.
5. **All 12 keys.** Remaining scales and arpeggios. Play I–IV–V–I and ii–V–I in every key, transposing around the circle. Ear: descending and harmonic intervals, inversions, 3–5 note melodic dictation.
6. **Colour.** Secondary dominants (V/V, V/vi), modal mixture (iv, ♭VI, ♭VII), pentatonic and blues scales, Mixolydian/Dorian/Lydian as pop flavours. Slash-chord bass lines and left-hand patterns. Ear: chromatic degrees and borrowed chords.
7. **Ongoing.** 10–20 minute interleaved sessions, tempo ladders that reach and pass the target, and spaced-repetition review of facts.</result>

## 1. Morse learning engine

Files: `.../firmware/morse/learn.h`, `learn.c`, `LEARNING.md`, `README.md`, `app.h`, `app.c`, `content.h`, `content.c`, `words.tsv`, `fm1.toml`, `tests/basic.txt`, `tests/morse_test.c`, `web/index.html`; `.../docs/dev/morse.md`; `.../host/morse/PROTOCOL.md`, `progress.py`.

**Method: Koch order plus Leitner boxes, counted in rounds rather than days.** It is not FSRS or SM-2.
- **Two cards per character**: recognise and send. Each card sits in a box from 0 to 5, and box n comes due every 2^n rounds (`learn.h:2-5`, `learn.c:58-65`).
- **Rounds, not days**: the FM-1 has no clock that survives power-off (`LEARNING.md:80`, `morse.md:78`). A host-supplied date is on the roadmap (`morse.md:411`).
- **New items**: they open in fixed LCWO Koch order, 5 at a time (`LN_GROUP`), at most 3 new per round (`learn.h:17-21`, `learn.c:7`, `learn.c:177-184`). The next group opens only when every open item is at recognise ≥2 and send ≥1 (`learn.c:325-328`).
- **Building a round**: new and due cards come first, sorted by lowest box and then longest wait. Weak cards (box 0–1) are repeated later in the same round, and spare slots are filled with the weakest non-due cards (`learn.c:186-255`).
- **Answers**:
  - Wrong: box goes to 0 and the card is asked again at the end of the round. Right on that second try does not promote it (`learn.c:287-309`).
  - `LN_ALMOST`: box unchanged, card re-asked (`learn.c:292-298`).
  - Streak: counts consecutive rounds at ≥80% (`learn.c:321-322`).
- **Card types**: `CARD_NEW`, `HEAR_CHOOSE`, `HEAR_KEY`, `SEE_KEY`, `CODE_CHOOSE`, `LIGHT_CHOOSE` (`learn.h:25-33`). Boxes below 3 use pick-one-of-four; box 3 and up switch to recall (`learn.c:85-94`).
- **Wrong options**: the three distractors are the most similar-sounding codes plus some randomness (`ln_alike`/`ln_options`, `learn.c:98-124`). This is the part to reuse for confusable intervals or chords.
- **Other tools**: a placement test (`learn.c:151-168`, `422-443`) and hand edits: set level, open groups, step everything back a box (`learn.h:86-95`).
- **Round size**: 10–30 cards, default 20 (`app.c:54`, `app.c:93`), capped at 24 by `LN_CARDS_MAX/2` (`learn.c:170-173`).
- The engine has no platform calls and no libc (`learn.h:8`).

**State and persistence**
- `ln_state_t` (`learn.h:35-43`) is about 260 B in RAM: per card, a `box` u8 plus a `last` round u16.
- The saved record is `rec_t` = magic `"MOR1"`, version, size, `set_t` settings and `ln_state_t` (`app.c:43-70`). It is about 280 B (`morse.md:315`; the README says "about 300", `README.md:132`).
- Map: `enum { OBJ_PANEL, OBJ_MORSE, OBJ_NOBJ }`, `APP_STORE_MAP {0xDC000u, 0xDA000u}` (`app.h:20-21`).
- Saved via `plat_store_save` (`app.c:112-120`):
  - at round end or when leaving a round (`app.c:794-795`, `905-906`);
  - after a confirmed question (`app.c:1018-1036`);
  - 3 s after a settings change (`app.c:3049-3050`).
- Loaded and validated at boot, falling back to defaults if invalid (`app.c:2987-2994`).

**Quiz input (PRACTICE)**
- The four answers are piano keys E4 F4 G4 A4: `CHOICE_KEY[4] = {11, 12, 14, 16}` (`app.c:241`). Those keys light up and the selected one blinks (`app.c:1964-1966`). Their note names are drawn under each choice box (`app.c:2314-2326`).
- Alternative: turn `SELECT` to move and press `SEL` to pick (`app.c:1605-1606`, `1567-1568`).
- Any key advances a NEW card (`app.c:1509-1510`).
- `SEL` on a keyed card means "don't know" (`app.c:1570`).
- `PLAY` starts a round or replays the prompt (`app.c:1524-1531`).
- `SEQ` peeks at the code (`app.c:1852-1859`).
- Any key skips the wait on the result screen (`app.c:1515-1516`).
- The full control table is at `README.md:34-57`.

**UI structure: a hand-written state machine**
- Pages are `PG_MENU…PG_SET` (`app.c:124`), switched by the `ALGO` encoder or the `HOME` menu (`app.c:1917-1922`, `1841`, `set_page` at `704-718`).
- PRACTICE has sub-states `PS_START → PS_CARD → PS_RESULT → PS_DONE` (`app.c:125`, `775-937`).
- Modal `ASK_*` questions (`app.c:225`) block every input except `PLAY` = yes and `HOME` = no (`app.c:1799-1814`).
- Screen layout:
  - Header: 240×32 at y=0 (`app.c:2017-2053`).
  - Main area: 176 px, drawn in two 88-px halves (`app.c:2793-2804`).
  - Footer: 240×32 at y=208 (`app.c:2860-2925`).
- Partial redraws use `R_*` flags (`app.c:196`).
- `app_frame` is the main loop (`app.c:3016-3055`). The 1 kHz `app_tick` handles keying and MIDI (`app.c:447-487`).

**Content is not compiled from TSV**
- `content.c` is hand-written C lists: top-100 words, CW abbreviations, sayings (`content.c:8-45`). Lines are generated at runtime with a seeded RNG (`content.h:2-24`).
- `words.tsv` holds only the screen reader's words (`words.tsv:2`). fm1-base's `gen_words.py` turns it into `ann_words.h` and `web/words/*.json`.
- fm1-base does support build-time generators through `fm1.toml gen = [...]` (fm1-base `tools/build.py:227-228`, `443-449`). Morse doesn't use it; a music app could generate its chord and scale tables this way.

**Tests**
- `tests/basic.txt` (843 lines) is a host-simulator script. Its header lists the page numbers (`basic.txt:1-4`).
- Commands used: `wait`, `shot X.png`, `expect <what> <n>`, `tap BTN`, `turn ENC N`, `key K down|up`, `tapkey`, `sysex`, `expect_sysex`, `expect_out`, `midi`, `reboot` (a persistence check at lines 499 and 840).
- The app adds its own commands via `APP_HOST_CMD`: `answer right|wrong`, `answer_all`, `setcard`, `setstrict`, `sendkeys`, `expect_text` (`app.c:3196-3286`). It adds its own `expect` keys via `APP_HOST_EXPECT` (`app.c:3061-3180`).
- The simulator's full command list is in fm1-base `host/plat_host.c:9-60`. It can also record WAV (`wav FILE`).
- Platform-free unit tests are in `tests/morse_test.c`, using a `CHECK` macro (`morse_test.c:10-11`). `just morse-unit` runs them: 3,016 checks (`morse.md:365`).

**Host backup and restore**
- Morse uses its own SysEx protocol over `hostlink` with id `4D 4F` (`app.c:3003`). It does not use fm1-base's generic `backup = true`.
- Wire format: a format byte, `ln_blob` (259 B, `learn.h:96-100`) and a CRC-16, 262 B in total. It is cut into 6 chunks of 49 B, each 7-bit packed (`app.c:22-27`, `1063-1125`).
- Load path: `T_PROG_LOAD` → `prog_in` checks chunk order, CRC and `ln_unblob` → an `ASK_LOAD` question → `PLAY` loads, then `T_PROG_DONE` is sent (`app.c:1127-1165`, `1006-1060`).
- Host side: JSON `"fm1-morse-progress"` v1 (`progress.py:1-50`, `PROTOCOL.md:57-74`), run with `just morse-backup` / `morse-restore` (`justfile:305-310`). Also `web/index.html` over Web MIDI.

**Design notes**
- `morse.md` covers prior art (`7-15`), the learning design (`69-133`), backup (`134-148`), timing (`305-311`), flash (`313-324`), sizes (`326-337`), verification (`339-370`) and the backlog. The backlog explains why adding items forces a record-format bump (`morse.md:419`).

## 2. Audio

Files: `.../firmware/morse/tone.c`, `tone.h`; `.../third_party/fm1-base/README.md`, `DESIGN.md`, `include/plat.h`, `include/fm1b_config.h`, `include/fastmath.h`, `device/unity.c`, `bsp/docs/BOARD_IO.md`, `template/app.c`, `lib/touch.h`; `.../firmware/common/chime.c`.

- **fm1-base has no synth engine, voice allocator or sampler.** The app writes every sample itself in `app_render(int32_t *lr, uint32_t n, uint32_t master_q12)`: 24-bit stereo in Q23, n = `APP_BLOCK` frames (`DESIGN.md:61-63`, `BOARD_IO.md:46-62`). Polyphony is whatever the app renders.
- **Existing voices**:
  - Morse `tone.c`: 2 sine voices with 5 ms smoothstep ramps. The gate is read once per block (`tone.h:2-21`, `tone.c:41-66`).
  - Template: 1 voice, last note wins, sine or triangle (template `app.c:27-88`).
  - `common/chime`: one 2-operator FM bell that plays a queue of up to 6 notes in sequence (MIDI note, ms each) (`chime.c:6-83`). That is effectively a monophonic arpeggio player.
- **Sample rate and latency**:
  - Nominal 44.1 kHz; the hardware actually runs at 44,117.647 Hz (`BOARD_IO.md:55-62`).
  - Default block 256 frames = 5.8 ms, configurable through `APP_BLOCK` (`fm1b_config.h:30-31`, `unity.c:15`). SLOOP 3 reportedly uses 64 (`docs/firmware/sloop/sloop3.md:22`, tagged as research).
- **CPU**: 360 MHz dual-core with a single-precision FPU (`docs/dev/tts.md:17`).
  - `fastmath.h` replaces libm (`fm_sinf`, `fm_exp2f`, …), and the build rejects `double` (`DESIGN.md:69`).
  - Audio code can run from RAM (`plat.h:20-45`).
  - Optional second core for the render (`README.md:45`, `plat.h:531-557`).
  - Load is visible through `plat_cpu_pct` and `plat_xruns`; an `APP_OVERLOAD` hook lets the app shed voices (`plat.h:493-499`, `612`).
  - A few sine or FM voices for chords are cheap by comparison: CTL-1 runs a full General MIDI synth (491 KB, `README.md:160`); SLOOP 2.8 has 8 voices and SLOOP 3 has 32 (research-tagged figures).
- **Timing for arpeggios**:
  - `APP_TICK` gives a 1 kHz timer interrupt (`plat.h:606`), shared with the main loop through `plat_lock`/`plat_unlock` (`plat.h:332-337`).
  - `plat_ticks24` is a 24 MHz counter (`plat.h:505-506`).
  - Note on/off flags set from the tick land with up to one block (5.8 ms) of jitter, like Morse's gate. For tight timing, schedule notes by sample count inside the render.
- **Samples**: you'd build them yourself, using `common/adpcm` (IMA 4-bit decoder) plus `plat_res` or `plat_data`. Voicelab already decodes in the audio interrupt and upsamples (`tts.md:23`, `87-92`).
- **MIDI**:
  - 4-byte USB-MIDI packets. `plat_midi_send(pkt, TO_USB|TO_BLE)` can be called from the main loop, the render or the tick; `plat_midi_in` reads USB, TRS (input only, there is no MIDI out jack) and BLE (`plat.h:96-122`).
  - BLE MIDI is optional (`README.md:28-33`). USB MIDI host mode lets the FM-1 drive a USB keyboard or synth directly (`plat.h:123-130`).
  - USB audio is on by default in both directions (`README.md:34-35`). The FM-1 is recordable over USB, and a computer can play through its speaker, which is how `vocab.md:7` plans to use host TTS.
- **Velocity and pressure**: `APP_TOUCH` turns them on (`lib/touch.h:3-15`). The 20 keys F3–C5 have velocity and pressure; the top 7 (C#5–G5) have velocity only. The ChoralRoot notes say "no velocity" (`docs/firmware/choralroot/index.md:60`), but that refers to ChoralRoot itself, which is Felucca-based.

  - There is no full framebuffer. You draw into a strip canvas of up to `APP_CANVAS_PX` (default 240×144) and blit it (`gfx.c:4-25`).
  - Primitives: `cv_begin`, `cv_rect`, `cv_line`, `cv_pset`, `cv_text`, `text_w`, `cv_blit`, `lcd_fill`, plus a 5-step palette (`gfx.c:27-120`, `213`, `294`).
  - **There is no circle or arc primitive.** A circle of fifths would be drawn with `cv_line`/`cv_pset` and `fm_sinf`/`fm_cosf`.
- **Fonts**:
  - Six roles from Barlow Semi Condensed (default) or Terminus. `T` is 10 px; `XS`, `S` and `B` are 12–15 px with ASCII 32–126; `M` (23 px) and `L` (31 px) have capitals and digits only unless `font_full` is set (`gen_font.py:25-41`, `62`; `build.py:48-55`).
  - **ASCII only, no ♯ or ♭** (`vocab.md:56`). Use `#` and `b`, or draw the symbols as bitmaps. Lowercase `b` is not available in the T, M and L roles by default.
- **Other I/O**: USB-C, TRS MIDI input and a 3.5 mm stereo output; no audio input and no clock that survives power-off (`docs/hardware/io.md:5-14`, `tts.md:21`).

## 4. Storage and flash budget

Files: `.../third_party/fm1-base/device/app.ld`, `tools/build.py`, `tools/lz4blk.py`, `tools/boot_pack.py`, `device/res.c`, `include/plat.h`, `README.md`; `.../docs/dev/morse.md`, `.../docs/dev/vocab.md`, `.../docs/hardware/flash-map.md`.

- **App slot**: 581,564 B = `0x8DFBC` (`app.ld:17`, `45`; checked at `build.py:298`, `1187-1188`). The firmware area is `0x04000–0x92FFF` (`flash-map.md:10`).
- **RAM**: 96 KB for `.data` + `.bss` and a 336 KB pool (`README.md:143-146`).
- **Morse 0.4**: 138,076 B of app code, `.data+.bss` 29,084 of 98,304 B, package 616,003 B (`morse.md:328-337`). That leaves about 440 KB of slot free.
- **Store objects**:
  - Each object is an A/B pair of 4 KiB sectors with a CRC, in the data area `0x97000–0xDFFFF` or the settings pair at `0xFC000`.
  - **Max 3,840 B per object** (`PLAT_STORE_MAX`). Pooled objects are possible (`plat.h:471-490`).
  - Big raw data goes through `plat_data*` in the same area and the XDATA windows (`plat.h:345-390`).
  - At Morse's 3 B per card, one object holds roughly 1,200 cards.
- **Coexisting with Morse**: Morse occupies `0xDA000–0xDBFFF` and the panel calibration sits at `0xDC000` (`flash-map.md:40-42`). A new app should pick other sectors if it is meant to leave Morse's progress intact.
- **Resource region**:
  - Set `fm1.toml resources = "FILE"` (requires `backup = true`) and define `APP_RES_BASE`/`APP_RES_SECTORS` in `app.h` (`build.py:118-125`).
  - The package carries it and the update loader writes it after the app. The app reads it in place with `plat_res(&len)`, which returns 0 if it is absent (`res.c:1-34`, `plat.h:413-417`).
  - The build bakes in its length and CRC, so changing the content means rebuilding (`vocab.md:85`).
- **`tools/lz4blk.py`**:
  - It is a host-side Python LZ4 block compressor and decompressor (`lz4blk.py:1-8`).
  - `build.py` uses it only to wrap the update loader (`build.py:295`, `517-528`).
  - fm1-base gives apps no C LZ4 decoder; an app would need its own.
  - Boot packing is LZMA and covers only `.ram_text` and `.data` (`boot_pack.py:1-30`).
- **Budget example**: the vocab page has a worked flash budget (`vocab.md:62-73`).

## 5. Shared code

Files: `.../firmware/common/README.md`, `hostlink.h`, `ledfx.h`, `chime.h`, `chime.c`, `lpc.h`, `adpcm.h`.

All MIT, included with `#include "x.c"` and `fm1.toml include = ["../common"]` (`README.md:16-32`). Morse carries its own copies of `hostlink` and `ledfx` in `firmware/morse/common/`; the README says to keep the two in sync (`README.md:33-37`).

| Module | What it offers |
|---|---|
| `hostlink` | SysEx framing `F0 7D id0 id1 ver type …`, HELLO and HEARTBEAT, host presence with a 10 s timeout, USB and BLE (BLE needs the own stack), `hl_send`, 64-byte payloads (`hostlink.h:1-65`) |
| `ledfx` | Off, glow, mid, lit, pulse, blink, double-blink and fast patterns per LED, turned into `plat_lights` calls once a frame (`ledfx.h`) |
| `chime` | 2-operator FM bell with a queue of up to 6 notes and preset figures, e.g. `DONE` = C5 E5 G5 (`chime.c:15-21`) |
| `lpc` | TMS5220 LPC speech decoder, 8 kHz (`lpc.h`) |
| `adpcm` | Streaming IMA ADPCM decoder in 256-byte blocks of 505 samples (`adpcm.h`) |

## 1. Morse learning engine

Files: `.../firmware/morse/learn.h`, `learn.c`, `LEARNING.md`, `README.md`, `app.h`, `app.c`, `content.h`, `content.c`, `words.tsv`, `fm1.toml`, `tests/basic.txt`, `tests/morse_test.c`, `web/index.html`; `.../docs/dev/morse.md`; `.../host/morse/PROTOCOL.md`, `progress.py`.

**Method: Koch order plus Leitner boxes, counted in rounds rather than days.** It is not FSRS or SM-2.
- **Two cards per character**: recognise and send. Each card sits in a box from 0 to 5, and box n comes due every 2^n rounds (`learn.h:2-5`, `learn.c:58-65`).
- **Rounds, not days**: the FM-1 has no clock that survives power-off (`LEARNING.md:80`, `morse.md:78`). A host-supplied date is on the roadmap (`morse.md:411`).
- **New items**: they open in fixed LCWO Koch order, 5 at a time (`LN_GROUP`), at most 3 new per round (`learn.h:17-21`, `learn.c:7`, `learn.c:177-184`). The next group opens only when every open item is at recognise ≥2 and send ≥1 (`learn.c:325-328`).
- **Building a round**: new and due cards come first, sorted by lowest box and then longest wait. Weak cards (box 0–1) are repeated later in the same round, and spare slots are filled with the weakest non-due cards (`learn.c:186-255`).
- **Answers**:
  - Wrong: box goes to 0 and the card is asked again at the end of the round. Right on that second try does not promote it (`learn.c:287-309`).
  - `LN_ALMOST`: box unchanged, card re-asked (`learn.c:292-298`).
  - Streak: counts consecutive rounds at ≥80% (`learn.c:321-322`).
- **Card types**: `CARD_NEW`, `HEAR_CHOOSE`, `HEAR_KEY`, `SEE_KEY`, `CODE_CHOOSE`, `LIGHT_CHOOSE` (`learn.h:25-33`). Boxes below 3 use pick-one-of-four; box 3 and up switch to recall (`learn.c:85-94`).
- **Wrong options**: the three distractors are the most similar-sounding codes plus some randomness (`ln_alike`/`ln_options`, `learn.c:98-124`). This is the part to reuse for confusable intervals or chords.
- **Other tools**: a placement test (`learn.c:151-168`, `422-443`) and hand edits: set level, open groups, step everything back a box (`learn.h:86-95`).
- **Round size**: 10–30 cards, default 20 (`app.c:54`, `app.c:93`), capped at 24 by `LN_CARDS_MAX/2` (`learn.c:170-173`).
- The engine has no platform calls and no libc (`learn.h:8`).

**State and persistence**
- `ln_state_t` (`learn.h:35-43`) is about 260 B in RAM: per card, a `box` u8 plus a `last` round u16.
- The saved record is `rec_t` = magic `"MOR1"`, version, size, `set_t` settings and `ln_state_t` (`app.c:43-70`). It is about 280 B (`morse.md:315`; the README says "about 300", `README.md:132`).
- Map: `enum { OBJ_PANEL, OBJ_MORSE, OBJ_NOBJ }`, `APP_STORE_MAP {0xDC000u, 0xDA000u}` (`app.h:20-21`).
- Saved via `plat_store_save` (`app.c:112-120`):
  - at round end or when leaving a round (`app.c:794-795`, `905-906`);
  - after a confirmed question (`app.c:1018-1036`);
  - 3 s after a settings change (`app.c:3049-3050`).
- Loaded and validated at boot, falling back to defaults if invalid (`app.c:2987-2994`).

**Quiz input (PRACTICE)**
- The four answers are piano keys E4 F4 G4 A4: `CHOICE_KEY[4] = {11, 12, 14, 16}` (`app.c:241`). Those keys light up and the selected one blinks (`app.c:1964-1966`). Their note names are drawn under each choice box (`app.c:2314-2326`).
- Alternative: turn `SELECT` to move and press `SEL` to pick (`app.c:1605-1606`, `1567-1568`).
- Any key advances a NEW card (`app.c:1509-1510`).
- `SEL` on a keyed card means "don't know" (`app.c:1570`).
- `PLAY` starts a round or replays the prompt (`app.c:1524-1531`).
- `SEQ` peeks at the code (`app.c:1852-1859`).
- Any key skips the wait on the result screen (`app.c:1515-1516`).
- The full control table is at `README.md:34-57`.

**UI structure: a hand-written state machine**
- Pages are `PG_MENU…PG_SET` (`app.c:124`), switched by the `ALGO` encoder or the `HOME` menu (`app.c:1917-1922`, `1841`, `set_page` at `704-718`).
- PRACTICE has sub-states `PS_START → PS_CARD → PS_RESULT → PS_DONE` (`app.c:125`, `775-937`).
- Modal `ASK_*` questions (`app.c:225`) block every input except `PLAY` = yes and `HOME` = no (`app.c:1799-1814`).
- Screen layout:
  - Header: 240×32 at y=0 (`app.c:2017-2053`).
  - Main area: 176 px, drawn in two 88-px halves (`app.c:2793-2804`).
  - Footer: 240×32 at y=208 (`app.c:2860-2925`).
- Partial redraws use `R_*` flags (`app.c:196`).
- `app_frame` is the main loop (`app.c:3016-3055`). The 1 kHz `app_tick` handles keying and MIDI (`app.c:447-487`).

**Content is not compiled from TSV**
- `content.c` is hand-written C lists: top-100 words, CW abbreviations, sayings (`content.c:8-45`). Lines are generated at runtime with a seeded RNG (`content.h:2-24`).
- `words.tsv` holds only the screen reader's words (`words.tsv:2`). fm1-base's `gen_words.py` turns it into `ann_words.h` and `web/words/*.json`.
- fm1-base does support build-time generators through `fm1.toml gen = [...]` (fm1-base `tools/build.py:227-228`, `443-449`). Morse doesn't use it; a music app could generate its chord and scale tables this way.

**Tests**
- `tests/basic.txt` (843 lines) is a host-simulator script. Its header lists the page numbers (`basic.txt:1-4`).
- Commands used: `wait`, `shot X.png`, `expect &lt;what&gt; &lt;n&gt;`, `tap BTN`, `turn ENC N`, `key K down|up`, `tapkey`, `sysex`, `expect_sysex`, `expect_out`, `midi`, `reboot` (a persistence check at lines 499 and 840).
- The app adds its own commands via `APP_HOST_CMD`: `answer right|wrong`, `answer_all`, `setcard`, `setstrict`, `sendkeys`, `expect_text` (`app.c:3196-3286`). It adds its own `expect` keys via `APP_HOST_EXPECT` (`app.c:3061-3180`).
- The simulator's full command list is in fm1-base `host/plat_host.c:9-60`. It can also record WAV (`wav FILE`).
- Platform-free unit tests are in `tests/morse_test.c`, using a `CHECK` macro (`morse_test.c:10-11`). `just morse-unit` runs them: 3,016 checks (`morse.md:365`).

**Host backup and restore**
- Morse uses its own SysEx protocol over `hostlink` with id `4D 4F` (`app.c:3003`). It does not use fm1-base's generic `backup = true`.
- Wire format: a format byte, `ln_blob` (259 B, `learn.h:96-100`) and a CRC-16, 262 B in total. It is cut into 6 chunks of 49 B, each 7-bit packed (`app.c:22-27`, `1063-1125`).
- Load path: `T_PROG_LOAD` → `prog_in` checks chunk order, CRC and `ln_unblob` → an `ASK_LOAD` question → `PLAY` loads, then `T_PROG_DONE` is sent (`app.c:1127-1165`, `1006-1060`).
- Host side: JSON `"fm1-morse-progress"` v1 (`progress.py:1-50`, `PROTOCOL.md:57-74`), run with `just morse-backup` / `morse-restore` (`justfile:305-310`). Also `web/index.html` over Web MIDI.

**Design notes**
- `morse.md` covers prior art (`7-15`), the learning design (`69-133`), backup (`134-148`), timing (`305-311`), flash (`313-324`), sizes (`326-337`), verification (`339-370`) and the backlog. The backlog explains why adding items forces a record-format bump (`morse.md:419`).
- `firmware/morse/docs/` holds only `screen.png` (the Hub card) and `screens/*.png` (29 simulator shots).

## 2. Audio

Files: `.../firmware/morse/tone.c`, `tone.h`; `.../third_party/fm1-base/README.md`, `DESIGN.md`, `include/plat.h`, `include/fm1b_config.h`, `include/fastmath.h`, `device/unity.c`, `bsp/docs/BOARD_IO.md`, `template/app.c`, `lib/touch.h`; `.../firmware/common/chime.c`.

- **fm1-base has no synth engine, voice allocator or sampler.** The app writes every sample itself in `app_render(int32_t *lr, uint32_t n, uint32_t master_q12)`: 24-bit stereo in Q23, n = `APP_BLOCK` frames (`DESIGN.md:61-63`, `BOARD_IO.md:46-62`). Polyphony is whatever the app renders.
- **Existing voices**:
  - Morse `tone.c`: 2 sine voices with 5 ms smoothstep ramps. The gate is read once per block (`tone.h:2-21`, `tone.c:41-66`).
  - Template: 1 voice, last note wins, sine or triangle (template `app.c:27-88`).
  - `common/chime`: one 2-operator FM bell that plays a queue of up to 6 notes in sequence (MIDI note, ms each) (`chime.c:6-83`). That is effectively a monophonic arpeggio player.
- **Sample rate and latency**:
  - Nominal 44.1 kHz; the hardware actually runs at 44,117.647 Hz (`BOARD_IO.md:55-62`).
  - Default block 256 frames = 5.8 ms, configurable through `APP_BLOCK` (`fm1b_config.h:30-31`, `unity.c:15`). SLOOP 3 reportedly uses 64 (`docs/firmware/sloop/sloop3.md:22`, tagged as research).
- **CPU**: 360 MHz dual-core with a single-precision FPU (`docs/dev/tts.md:17`).
  - `fastmath.h` replaces libm (`fm_sinf`, `fm_exp2f`, …), and the build rejects `double` (`DESIGN.md:69`).
  - Audio code can run from RAM (`plat.h:20-45`).
  - Optional second core for the render (`README.md:45`, `plat.h:531-557`).
  - Load is visible through `plat_cpu_pct` and `plat_xruns`; an `APP_OVERLOAD` hook lets the app shed voices (`plat.h:493-499`, `612`).
  - A few sine or FM voices for chords are cheap by comparison: CTL-1 runs a full General MIDI synth (491 KB, `README.md:160`); SLOOP 2.8 has 8 voices and SLOOP 3 has 32 (research-tagged figures).
- **Timing for arpeggios**:
  - `APP_TICK` gives a 1 kHz timer interrupt (`plat.h:606`), shared with the main loop through `plat_lock`/`plat_unlock` (`plat.h:332-337`).
  - `plat_ticks24` is a 24 MHz counter (`plat.h:505-506`).
  - Note on/off flags set from the tick land with up to one block (5.8 ms) of jitter, like Morse's gate. For tight timing, schedule notes by sample count inside the render.
- **Samples**: you'd build them yourself, using `common/adpcm` (IMA 4-bit decoder) plus `plat_res` or `plat_data`. Voicelab already decodes in the audio interrupt and upsamples (`tts.md:23`, `87-92`).
- **MIDI**:
  - 4-byte USB-MIDI packets. `plat_midi_send(pkt, TO_USB|TO_BLE)` can be called from the main loop, the render or the tick; `plat_midi_in` reads USB, TRS (input only, there is no MIDI out jack) and BLE (`plat.h:96-122`).
  - BLE MIDI is optional (`README.md:28-33`). USB MIDI host mode lets the FM-1 drive a USB keyboard or synth directly (`plat.h:123-130`).
  - USB audio is on by default in both directions (`README.md:34-35`). The FM-1 is recordable over USB, and a computer can play through its speaker, which is how `vocab.md:7` plans to use host TTS.
- **Velocity and pressure**: `APP_TOUCH` turns them on (`lib/touch.h:3-15`). The 20 keys F3–C5 have velocity and pressure; the top 7 (C#5–G5) have velocity only. The ChoralRoot notes say "no velocity" (`docs/firmware/choralroot/index.md:60`), but that refers to ChoralRoot itself, which is Felucca-based.

## 3. Hardware I/O

Files: `.../third_party/fm1-base/include/plat.h`, `device/gfx.c`, `device/lcd.c`, `tools/gen_font.py`, `tools/build.py`, `bsp/docs/BOARD_IO.md`; `.../firmware/common/ledfx.h`; `.../docs/hardware/io.md`, `.../docs/dev/vocab.md`.

- **Keys**: `NKEYS 27`, F3–G5 (`plat.h:53`): 16 white and 11 black (`plat.h:55-56`). Key 0 is MIDI 53 (F3) and key 26 is MIDI 79 (G5) (Morse `app.c:298-301`, template `app.c:272`).
- **Buttons**: 14. `B_FX, B_SEL, B_ENV, B_LFO, B_EDIT, B_GLO, B_HOME, B_SAVE, B_ARP, B_SEQ, B_PLAY, B_REC, B_OCTDN, B_OCTUP` (`plat.h:49-50`).
- **Encoders**: 7 detent encoders, `EN_SELECT, EN_ALGO, EN_PRESET, EN_K1..K4`, read with `plat_enc` (`plat.h:51`, `63`). Plus the `MASTER` pot via `plat_master` (`plat.h:64`).
- **Unused in Morse**: ENV, LFO, EDIT, GLO, SAVE, ARP and the PRESET encoder (`app.c:1939`). They are free for a new app.
- **LEDs**:
  - One single-colour LED per key and per button; PLAY also has a green LED (`LED_PLAY_GREEN`).
  - Levels are off, glow, mid and lit (`plat.h:77-94`), plus any dim brightness via `plat_dim_ns`.
  - `ledfx` adds pulse, blink, double-blink and fast patterns (`ledfx.h:1-31`).
  - ChoralRoot uses key LEDs to show a key: scale notes dim, tonic brighter (`docs/firmware/choralroot/tutorial.md:156`).
- **LCD**:
  - 240×240 ST7789V, RGB565 (16-bit colour) (`BOARD_IO.md:8-20`, `lcd.c:4`).
  - There is no full framebuffer. You draw into a strip canvas of up to `APP_CANVAS_PX` (default 240×144) and blit it (`gfx.c:4-25`).
  - Primitives: `cv_begin`, `cv_rect`, `cv_line`, `cv_pset`, `cv_text`, `text_w`, `cv_blit`, `lcd_fill`, plus a 5-step palette (`gfx.c:27-120`, `213`, `294`).
  - **There is no circle or arc primitive.** A circle of fifths would be drawn with `cv_line`/`cv_pset` and `fm_sinf`/`fm_cosf`.
- **Fonts**:
  - Six roles from Barlow Semi Condensed (default) or Terminus. `T` is 10 px; `XS`, `S` and `B` are 12–15 px with ASCII 32–126; `M` (23 px) and `L` (31 px) have capitals and digits only unless `font_full` is set (`gen_font.py:25-41`, `62`; `build.py:48-55`).
  - **ASCII only, no ♯ or ♭** (`vocab.md:56`). Use `#` and `b`, or draw the symbols as bitmaps. Lowercase `b` is not available in the T, M and L roles by default.
- **Other I/O**: USB-C, TRS MIDI input and a 3.5 mm stereo output; no audio input and no clock that survives power-off (`docs/hardware/io.md:5-14`, `tts.md:21`).

## 4. Storage and flash budget

Files: `.../third_party/fm1-base/device/app.ld`, `tools/build.py`, `tools/lz4blk.py`, `tools/boot_pack.py`, `device/res.c`, `include/plat.h`, `README.md`; `.../docs/dev/morse.md`, `.../docs/dev/vocab.md`, `.../docs/hardware/flash-map.md`.

- **App slot**: 581,564 B = `0x8DFBC` (`app.ld:17`, `45`; checked at `build.py:298`, `1187-1188`). The firmware area is `0x04000–0x92FFF` (`flash-map.md:10`).
- **RAM**: 96 KB for `.data` + `.bss` and a 336 KB pool (`README.md:143-146`).
- **Morse 0.4**: 138,076 B of app code, `.data+.bss` 29,084 of 98,304 B, package 616,003 B (`morse.md:328-337`). That leaves about 440 KB of slot free.
- **Store objects**:
  - Each object is an A/B pair of 4 KiB sectors with a CRC, in the data area `0x97000–0xDFFFF` or the settings pair at `0xFC000`.
  - **Max 3,840 B per object** (`PLAT_STORE_MAX`). Pooled objects are possible (`plat.h:471-490`).
  - Big raw data goes through `plat_data*` in the same area and the XDATA windows (`plat.h:345-390`).
  - At Morse's 3 B per card, one object holds roughly 1,200 cards.
- **Coexisting with Morse**: Morse occupies `0xDA000–0xDBFFF` and the panel calibration sits at `0xDC000` (`flash-map.md:40-42`). A new app should pick other sectors if it is meant to leave Morse's progress intact.
- **Resource region**:
  - Set `fm1.toml resources = "FILE"` (requires `backup = true`) and define `APP_RES_BASE`/`APP_RES_SECTORS` in `app.h` (`build.py:118-125`).
  - The package carries it and the update loader writes it after the app. The app reads it in place with `plat_res(&amp;len)`, which returns 0 if it is absent (`res.c:1-34`, `plat.h:413-417`).
  - The build bakes in its length and CRC, so changing the content means rebuilding (`vocab.md:85`).
- **`tools/lz4blk.py`**:
  - It is a host-side Python LZ4 block compressor and decompressor (`lz4blk.py:1-8`).
  - `build.py` uses it only to wrap the update loader (`build.py:295`, `517-528`).
  - fm1-base gives apps no C LZ4 decoder; an app would need its own.
  - Boot packing is LZMA and covers only `.ram_text` and `.data` (`boot_pack.py:1-30`).
- **Budget example**: the vocab page has a worked flash budget (`vocab.md:62-73`).

## 5. Shared code

Files: `.../firmware/common/README.md`, `hostlink.h`, `ledfx.h`, `chime.h`, `chime.c`, `lpc.h`, `adpcm.h`.

All MIT, included with `#include "x.c"` and `fm1.toml include = ["../common"]` (`README.md:16-32`). Morse carries its own copies of `hostlink` and `ledfx` in `firmware/morse/common/`; the README says to keep the two in sync (`README.md:33-37`).

| Module | What it offers |
|---|---|
| `hostlink` | SysEx framing `F0 7D id0 id1 ver type …`, HELLO and HEARTBEAT, host presence with a 10 s timeout, USB and BLE (BLE needs the own stack), `hl_send`, 64-byte payloads (`hostlink.h:1-65`) |
| `ledfx` | Off, glow, mid, lit, pulse, blink, double-blink and fast patterns per LED, turned into `plat_lights` calls once a frame (`ledfx.h`) |
| `chime` | 2-operator FM bell with a queue of up to 6 notes and preset figures, e.g. `DONE` = C5 E5 G5 (`chime.c:15-21`) |
| `lpc` | TMS5220 LPC speech decoder, 8 kHz (`lpc.h`) |
| `adpcm` | Streaming IMA ADPCM decoder in 256-byte blocks of 505 samples (`adpcm.h`) |
